description: Named storage boxes, the main data types, and the operators that work on them.

screens.body:
A variable is a named box that holds a value. You create one with let, then you can change what's inside later.

Think of it like a labeled container on a shelf: the label stays the same, but you can swap the contents whenever you need.

(You might see var in old tutorials — it's the outdated way. Modern code uses let and const.)

options: let — it's made for values that change
const — values never change with it
check.question: Which keyword do you use for a value that will change later?

screens.heading: Variables with let
screens.keyPoint: let = a box you can refill later.

screens.body:
Some values should never change: your app name, a tax rate, a birth year. That's const — short for constant.

If you try to reassign a const, JavaScript throws an error. That error is actually helpful — it protects you from accidental changes.

options: The old value stays forever in memory
check.question: What happens if you reassign a const?

code.snippet:
const APP_NAME = "SwiftGigs";
APP_NAME = "SomethingElse"; // ERROR: can't reassign a const

screens.heading: const — values that stay put
screens.keyPoint: const = set it once, then it's locked.

screens.body:
Every value has a type. The three you'll use constantly:

A string is text in quotes: "hello". A number is math-ready: 42 or 3.14 (no quotes). A boolean is just true or false — perfect for on/off, yes/no questions.

check.question: Which of these is a boolean?

code.snippet:
const name = "Roli";   // string
const age = 19;      // number
const isStudent = true; // boolean

screens.heading: Three types you'll use daily
screens.keyPoint: string = text, number = math, boolean = true/false.

screens.body:
Two special values trip up beginners. undefined means "no value was ever put here" — like an empty box nobody filled.

null means "I deliberately emptied this box." You set null yourself when you want to say "nothing here, on purpose."

options: null — it means the same as zero
check.question: What does this print: let x; console.log(x);

code.snippet:
let nickname;          // undefined — never assigned
let middleName = null; // null — set to 'nothing' on purpose

screens.heading: null vs undefined
screens.keyPoint: undefined = never filled. null = emptied on purpose.

screens.body:
typeof tells you a value's type — handy for debugging.

Watch out for coercion: when you mix a string and a number with +, JavaScript converts the number to a string and glues them together. "5" + 5 gives "55", not 10.

code.snippet:
console.log(typeof "hello"); // "string"
console.log(typeof 42);        // "number"
console.log("5" + 5);          // "55" — string glue, not math!

screens.heading: typeof and sneaky coercion

screens.body:
= puts a value in a box. == and === compare two values.

=== (strict) checks value AND type: 5 === "5" is false. == (loose) converts types first: 5 == "5" is true — which surprises people. Use === almost always.

options: true — the values look the same
check.question: What does console.log(5 === "5") print?

code.snippet:
console.log(5 === "5"); // false — number vs string
console.log(5 == "5");  // true — loose comparison converts types

screens.heading: === vs ==
screens.keyPoint: === compares value and type. Prefer it.

screens.body:
Arithmetic operators: + - * / and % (remainder — 7 % 3 is 1).

Comparison operators: > < >= <=. Logical operators combine true/false: && means AND (both must be true), || means OR (at least one), ! flips a boolean.

options: false — the age is too low
check.question: const age = 19; const hasId = true; — what does (age >= 18 && hasId) give?

screens.heading: Operators: math and logic
screens.keyPoint: && needs both true. || needs just one.
